claim: A subscription cancel flow save rate of about 15% is good, 20% is strong, and under 10% needs work; route each cancel reason to a matching save action.
body: The cancel flow is the sequence a subscriber sees in the portal after clicking cancel. One example flow saved 14.6% of attempted cancels; the speaker sets 15% as a good benchmark, 20% as strong, and below 10% as needing work. Structure: open with a splash screen, ideally a short founder video restating the mission, that steers towards delaying rather than cancelling; if there is a loyalty programme, show the points they would lose. Then ask why, and branch: too much product goes to skip or change next order date (the most common reason); want a different product goes to swap; do not like the taste goes to swap flavour or product; taking a break goes to skip; too expensive goes to a discount, optionally segmented further; plus an edit-frequency option. After a completed cancel, send one or two plain-text emails keyed to the stated reason with a reactivate link; expect little from these, because the customer has just refused every offer. How to apply: build the branches in your subscription app (Skio, Recharge, Loop), report save rate monthly by reason, and fix the weakest branch first.
conditions: Subscription apps that support cancel-reason branching and in-flow offers.
fails_when: Flows that make cancelling hard or hidden risk breaching click-to-cancel and auto-renewal rules; high save rates driven by skips can just defer churn, so check revenue per saved subscriber.
numbers: 14.6% save rate example
15% good, 20% strong, under 10% needs work

claim: Adding a one-minute founder video splash screen to the subscription cancel page took struggling brands from a 5-6% save rate to about 15%.
body: Holman's first fix for every brand that arrives with a weak cancel flow is a splash screen on the cancel page showing a short video from the founder, or a brand spokesperson if there is no founder persona. Brands arriving at a 5 to 6% save rate typically jump about 10 points, to around 15%, from this step alone. The video is about one minute: thanks for trying the product, a reminder of the mission, empathy, and a plain statement that the customer can adjust, delay or swap, and is welcome back whenever they leave. Splash screens are now supported by the main portals (Skio pioneered it, Recharge and Stay followed). What follows the video was tested: a skip button raised save rate but deferred revenue, so delay actions are preferred; if the common reason is price, a discount can sit there. He offers a script template on his site and suggests drafting it with AI from the brand's website. How to apply: record the video, add it as the first cancel-flow step, and compare save rate and revenue per attempted cancel for 30 days before and after.
conditions: Subscription brands on portals supporting cancel-flow splash media (Skio, Recharge, Stay, Loop); founder or face of brand available.
fails_when: Brands already saving 15-20% will not see a 10-point jump; a video that delays or obstructs cancellation can conflict with click-to-cancel rules, so the cancel path must stay clear.
numbers: save rate 5-6% to about 15% after founder video
video length about 1 minute

claim: For products without an immediate effect, frame a 90-day trial at onboarding: a prove-it challenge, a day-0 before photo, or a reward for logging daily use.
body: Holman's core onboarding rule is product adoption: the billing reminder and portal matter little if customers never use the product properly. His examples. X Endurance, a CrossFit supplement, tells buyers not to start immediately: do the week's big workout without it, take it for seven days, then repeat the same workout, inviting the customer to prove the claim; he still buys from them three years later. Skincare and hormone or menopause supplements, which take weeks to show results, ask for a before photo on day 0 and another at day 30, or offer a gift for sending before and after photos at day 14 and day 90, which sets the expectation that judgement waits about three months. A matcha brand's fold-out insert on brewing the perfect first cup created a memorable first use; a sleep supplement with no timing instructions forced him to search. Space Goods learned from customers how to make the best mushroom coffee and put it in onboarding, and retention improved. Also: include extra flavour samples in the first box (people who dislike their flavour never return, while flavour switchers are higher LTV). Avoid sales and cross-sell emails in onboarding; put cross-sells as samples in the next order instead.
conditions: Consumables whose benefit appears over weeks (supplements, skincare, hormone support) or that need a technique to use well.
fails_when: Products with an immediate, obvious effect where a challenge adds friction; inserts and samples add per-order cost that must be checked against the retention gained.
numbers: 7-day prove-it challenge (X Endurance)
before photos at day 0 and day 30, or day 14 and day 90

claim: In subscription cancel flows, a bigger discount on the next order saves more cancels than gifts; keep 6 to 7 cancel reasons and split vague ones by intent.
body: Although Holman dislikes discounting at acquisition, he calls discounts in the cancel flow the most effective save lever: in his tests gifts can work but save fewer than larger discounts, and a discount on this order beats a discount spread over time. Brands that say margins are too thin should compare a move from a 20% to a 30% save offer, an extra 10% of one order, with losing the subscriber entirely. Keep the reason list to six or seven options; each month move the one or two least-chosen into Other, then add more specific reasons. Split vague reasons by intent so copy fits: too expensive can mean not enough value seen (answer with education on why it is worth it and that cheaper alternatives cost more over time) or budget really changed (answer with empathy and a 40-50% off next order). Too much product can mean never started or wrong schedule (answer with a frequency change). At larger scale, segment offers by month of subscription, product or basket size, using flat-dollar offers such as $20 off only on baskets over $100. Feed reasons back into onboarding. ProsperStack is named for more control than in-app flows.
conditions: Subscription apps with branching cancel flows; brands with enough monthly cancels to read reason-level save rates.
fails_when: Margins so thin that a 30-50% next-order discount loses money even if the subscriber stays one more cycle; customers trained to threaten cancellation for a discount, visible as repeat cancel attempts.
numbers: save offer 20% vs 30%
6 to 7 cancel reasons
40-50% off next order for budget-changed segment
$20 flat offer only for baskets over $100

claim: Remove indefinite pauses (about 10% ever reactivate) and keep skip or delay up to 30 days; subscribers who adjusted frequency three times had 200% higher LTV.
body: The host and Holman agree on portal controls. Open-ended pauses are bad: the subscriber sits in limbo, often opted out of marketing, producing no revenue, and only around 10% ever reactivate. A pause that auto-resumes is really a delay and should be named that. Allow a single skip and delays of two or four weeks (about 30 days at most, longer for very large packs such as a big protein bag), and if a subscriber keeps skipping, let them cancel so they enter win-back and re-engagement marketing instead of limbo. By contrast, frequency changes should be easy and intuitive: a study Holman ran at the subscription app Autoship Cloud found subscribers who adjusted frequency three times had about 200% higher LTV than other subscribers, because they found a cadence that fits (his own seven-week razor cadence at Dollar Shave Club is the example). He also tested paying subscribers to pull orders forward during a sale (a bonus for clicking get now), since a skip only defers revenue. How to apply: disable or rename pause in the portal, cap delay length, surface edit frequency with common intervals, and track reactivation from any paused cohort.
conditions: Subscription consumables on portals that allow configuring pause, skip, delay and frequency options.
fails_when: Seasonal or travel-driven products where a long pause genuinely precedes return; the 200% LTV link is correlational (engaged subscribers adjust more), so forcing adjustments will not create it.
numbers: about 10% reactivation from indefinite pauses
delay cap about 30 days
3 frequency adjustments = about 200% higher LTV (Autoship Cloud study)

claim: Unannounced second-order gifts rarely pay: 900 renewing subscribers times a $2-5 gift costs about $2,000 for perhaps 45 extra orders; announce gifts at acquisition or target at-risk cohorts.
body: Holman is contrarian on post-purchase gift roadmaps pushed by subscription apps. In his tests, a 1,000-person cohort where 90% reach month two means 900 gifts at $2 to $5 each, roughly $2,000 or more. Even a 5% retention lift adds about 45 orders, which often does not repay the gift cost, and most recipients would have renewed anyway. Gifts earn their cost in two cases. First, when they are part of the acquisition offer and communicated throughout: Everyday Dose and Elevate show the gift ladder on the product page, then onboarding emails carry a banner such as free gift in your next order, and the billing reminder is framed around it. Second, when targeted at a cohort with higher VIP potential or at subscribers identified as at risk. A newer tactic: a click-to-redeem gift in the billing reminder, tagging clickers, since few people claim a gift and then cancel before it ships; or a portal pop-up shown only in the window between reminder and charge. How to apply: before launching a gift roadmap, estimate gift cost per cohort against the orders it must add, and only run it if it is visible at purchase and in every pre-charge message. The WellCopy host recommends gifts at months 2, 4 and 6, so test both.
conditions: Subscription brands considering surprise or milestone gifts after purchase.
fails_when: Gifts that are cheap cross-sell samples double as product expansion and can pay through later add-on revenue; brands with very high month-2 churn may see a larger lift than 5%.
numbers: 1,000 cohort, 900 reach month 2, $2-5 gift = about $2,000
5% lift = about 45 extra orders

claim: 71% of consumers say a poor return makes them less likely to buy again (NRF and Happy Returns 2025, n=2,006); fast refunds and exchange-first portals protect repeat rate.
body: The playbook treats returns as a retention fork rather than a cost line. Data: the NRF and Happy Returns 2025 Retail Returns Landscape (2,006 consumers) found about 71% are less likely to shop again after a poor return, up from 67% in 2024, and 80% tell friends and family; 76% are more likely to choose a retailer offering instant refund or exchange (NRF); a vendor (Narvar) reports 77% of shoppers with a good return would shop again. US returns were forecast at 849.9 billion USD in 2025, a 15.8% rate. Plays: 1) Self-service returns portal. 2) Measure return-to-refund time from the customer's request, not the warehouse scan, and shorten it. 3) Default to exchange or store credit to keep revenue, with refund still easy. 4) 'Keep it' refunds for low-value items when reverse logistics costs more than the item, capped by value and watched for serial abusers. 5) Check in a few days after delivery ('did it fit, did it work') to catch problems before they become returns. 6) Success test: repeat rate among customers who returned something matches or beats that of non-returners.
conditions: DTC brands with meaningful return volume (apparel, footwear, beauty, home); US data, likely similar in UK and EU.
fails_when: Categories with high return abuse or very thin margins, where instant refunds before inspection create losses; marketplaces or regions with mandated return terms that limit policy choices.

claim: A branded unboxing moment costs under 0.50 USD per order, mid-tier 1.50 to 3, premium 2.80 to 4.50; budget about 2 to 5% of product cost.
body: Cost benchmarks compiled in the playbook for designing the delivery peak: sticker 0.04 to 0.05 USD, tissue 0.05 to 0.15 USD per sheet, thank-you card about 0.10 USD; a basic branded moment (tissue, sticker, card) under 0.50 USD per order; a mid-tier experience (printed box, tissue, card, sticker) about 1.50 to 3.00 USD; a full custom premium experience 2.80 to 4.50 USD. Rule of thumb: spend 2 to 5% of product cost on packaging. Packaging inserts are reported to have about a 95% open rate against about 20% for email, so an insert with a QR code to a 60-second setup video or first-use guide is a cheap way to get customers to first value and cut support. Watch the per-order arithmetic: inserts scale with every order, so a 0.60 to 0.80 USD insert stack becomes material at around 2,000 orders a month. What works: a relevant sample matched to the purchase, a hand-signed note that names the item. What feels cheap: irrelevant samples, form letters pretending to be personal, a 'gift' that is a coupon. A widely repeated '26% more repeat purchases from memorable unboxing' figure is a vendor claim; measure repeat rate and UGC yourself.
conditions: DTC brands shipping their own orders with control over packaging; product prices where 2 to 5% covers at least the basic tier.
fails_when: Very low-price items where even 0.50 USD erodes margin, sustainability-led brands where extra layers draw criticism, or 3PL setups that charge extra per insert and pick step.

mid-tier 1.50 to 3.00 USD
premium 2.80 to 4.50 USD
packaging 2 to 5% of product cost

claim: Fix effort before adding delight: in a 75,000-customer study, 96% of high-effort service interactions produced disloyalty versus 9% of low-effort ones.
body: The 2010 HBR study 'Stop Trying to Delight Your Customers' (Dixon, Freeman, Toman; over 75,000 people in contact-centre and self-service interactions) found that reducing customer effort builds loyalty more than exceeding expectations: 96% of customers with high-effort interactions became more disloyal against 9% with low-effort ones, while 89 of 100 service heads said their strategy was to exceed expectations. Kahneman's peak-end research (people remember the most intense moment and the ending, not the average) supports designing a few peaks. The playbook reconciles them by journey stage: in problem moments (where is my order, returns, complaints, breakages) cut effort to one touch and never try to 'delight' a customer mid-problem; in discretionary moments (unboxing, first use, milestones) add a small planned peak. Build order: accurate delivery dates and proactive tracking, then fast kind returns, then an unboxing peak and first-use insert, then replenishment and second-purchase nudges, then quiz personalisation, and only then loyalty tiers and big surprise programmes. Delight layered on a broken base makes the failure more memorable. Track effort metrics (contact rate per order, refund cycle time) before delight metrics.
conditions: DTC brands deciding where to spend post-purchase budget; applies to all categories, strongest where service contacts are frequent.
fails_when: Brands whose operations are already low-effort and reliable, where the marginal gain shifts to peaks and community; the service research is from contact centres, not ecommerce specifically.
numbers: over 75,000 customers studied (Dixon et al., HBR 2010)
96% of high-effort versus 9% of low-effort interactions led to disloyalty
89 of 100 service heads aimed to exceed expectations

claim: Showing a specific delivery date instead of a vague range lifts conversion about 13 to 25%; pad the estimate so you usually beat it and keep accuracy above 90%.
body: The playbook cites Forrester (via Narvar) for a 13 to 25% conversion lift from specific delivery dates over vague ranges, and survey data that 75% of shoppers say a clear date influences purchase; one Narvar case lifted product-page conversion 19% and checkout 10%. These are mostly vendor case studies, so the direction is more reliable than the size. Precision now matters more than speed: delivery speed reportedly fell from shoppers' top delivery priority in 2022 to fifth by 2024, behind cost, transparency and reliability, and Narvar's 2025 survey of 3,461 US consumers found 74% received a package later than estimated in the past year. Method: 1) Build the estimate from your real lane and carrier transit data plus handling time, not the carrier's ideal service level. 2) Pad it slightly so most orders arrive early, which turns delivery into a small peak. 3) Show it on the product page and in checkout. 4) Track delivery estimate accuracy: orders delivered within the promised window divided by orders shipped; aim above 90% (vendor case work holds above 95%). 5) Pair with proactive delay messages.
conditions: DTC brands shipping from their own warehouse or a 3PL with trackable lanes; US, UK and similar markets.
fails_when: Fulfilment times are erratic (made-to-order, cross-border, pre-orders), so a precise date will often be missed and harm trust more than a range; over-padding can lose buyers who need speed.
numbers: 13 to 25% conversion lift for specific dates (Forrester via Narvar)
Narvar case: +19% product-page, +10% checkout conversion
74% of 3,461 US consumers got a late package in the past year (Narvar 2025)
delivery estimate accuracy target above 90%

claim: The service recovery paradox is rare: in an 11,000-plus interview banking study, only 5.4% of customers with a problem rated the recovery much better than expected.
body: The idea that a brilliantly fixed problem makes a customer more loyal than one who never had a problem is real but rare and conditional. Michel and Meuter ('The service recovery paradox: true but overrated?', Journal of Service Management, more than 11,000 banking interviews) found only 63 of 1,189 customers who had a problem perceived the recovery as much better than expected, 5.4%, and concluded that error-free service still beats recovery on overall satisfaction. The paradox appears mainly when the failure is not severe, it is the customer's first failure, and the recovery clearly exceeds expectations; organisational-learning research suggests it is strongest when the customer sees the firm took action to stop it recurring. Operating rule for a store: 1) Never plan around failures. 2) When something does go wrong (late, damaged, wrong item), reach out before the customer complains. 3) Empower support to resolve in one contact (refund, replacement, 'keep it, we'll send another'), and add a small gesture only after the fix. 4) Log the cause and tell the customer what changed. The downside of a poor recovery is much larger than the upside of a great one.
conditions: Any brand handling order failures; most relevant to support policy and refund authority.
fails_when: Severe or repeated failures, where no recovery restores loyalty; evidence is from banking, so effect sizes in ecommerce may differ.
numbers: 63 of 1,189 customers with a problem (5.4%) rated recovery much better than expected
study of more than 11,000 banking interviews

claim: WISMO contacts under 3% of orders is healthy, 3 to 8% normal but costly, above 8% structural; WISMO is often 30 to 50% of support tickets.
body: 'Where is my order' contacts are the largest avoidable support load in ecommerce. Vendor benchmarks compiled in the playbook (Clickpost, Gorgias, Pango, all flagged as vendor sources, consistent with each other) put WISMO at 30 to 50% of tickets in normal periods and 50 to 80% at peak; one helpdesk platform average is 18%. A per-order health scale (Pango): under 3% of orders generating a WISMO contact is healthy, 3 to 8% normal but expensive, above 8% a structural problem. Cost: agents spend 3 to 5 minutes per ticket, so 100 tickets a day consumes 5 to 8 agent-hours on lookups. Fix: 1) Show an accurate delivery date before purchase. 2) Push shipped, out-for-delivery, delivered and delayed messages by email and SMS. 3) Host tracking on a branded page rather than the carrier's. 4) Contact customers first when a parcel stalls. Vendors claim proactive updates cut WISMO by 50 to 72%; branded tracking tools start around 99 USD a month for 2,500 shipments. Move on to other retention work once WISMO is under about 5% of orders.
conditions: Shipping DTC brands with a support inbox; thresholds are per order, not per ticket.
fails_when: Brands with unreliable carriers or 3PLs, where better messaging exposes delays without fixing them; the fix there is fulfilment, not notifications. Benchmarks are vendor-sourced; measure your own.

claim: Before adding handwritten notes or free in-box gifts, compute the repeat-rate lift needed to break even (extra cost per order divided by repeat-order contribution) and run a holdout.
body: Delight inserts are sold with large numbers: handwritten-note vendors cite a 99 percent open rate, up to 37 percent higher retention and roughly double future spend. Those figures come from the vendors themselves and do not tell you whether your customers will reorder more. Treat the insert as a cost per order with a required effect. Steps: (1) cost it fully: a robot-written note through a service such as Handwrytten plus a small unannounced sample or gift typically lands in the low single dollars per order (the report's illustration uses about $3 for premium packaging and a note); include packing labour; (2) compute the break-even lift: cost per order divided by contribution per repeat order equals the extra repeat orders needed per customer (for example, $3 divided by $25 contribution means each recipient must place 0.12 more orders over the window); (3) target triggers rather than every order, such as a first order above a value threshold, a VIP tier, or a subscription anniversary, sent from Klaviyo or the helpdesk; (4) hold out a random 20 to 50 percent of eligible orders and compare 90- and 180-day repeat rate and spend; (5) keep it only if the measured lift clears break-even. Gifts work better unconditional and complementary (a sample of a related product) than as a discount code for the next order, which trains buyers to wait for deals.
conditions: DTC brands with repeatable products and enough eligible orders to compare cohorts (several hundred per arm); post-purchase inserts and notes.
fails_when: One-time-purchase categories with little repeat potential (mattresses, appliances), very low AOV where a $3 insert erases margin, and small order volumes where a holdout cannot show a difference; delighters also decay into expectations once customers come to rely on them.
numbers: illustrative cost about $3 per order for premium packaging plus robotic handwritten note
vendor-cited: 99 percent open rate, 80 percent read rate, up to 37 percent higher retention, about 100.5 percent more future spend (unverified)
worked break-even: $3 cost / $25 repeat contribution = 0.12 extra orders per customer

claim: Shoppers check tracking about 4.6 times per order; three proactive updates plus a branded tracking page are reported to cut 'where is my order' tickets 40 to 60%.
body: Most order-status anxiety sits between checkout and delivery. The source's baseline is three automatic messages: order confirmation with a clear delivery estimate, shipping confirmation with a tracking link, and an out-for-delivery notice with a delivery window. Operations literature it cites claims this alone can remove up to 80% of 'where is my order' (WISMO) contacts. The next step is replacing the carrier's tracking link with a branded tracking page on your own site. Customers look at tracking about 4.6 times per order, so the page gets repeat visits from people who just paid. Vendor-reported results: 40 to 60% fewer WISMO contacts and a 23 to 31% higher repeat purchase rate; Crystal Classics (Narvar, SMS updates for older buyers of luxury items) cut WISMO calls by up to 60% within weeks; IWA Wine Accessories cut WISMO by 47%; Bokksu's shipping emails reach 90%+ opens and 45.7% click-through. Put on the page: status, delivery window, carrier, a complementary product, loyalty sign-up, how-to content and an easy route to returns. Cost per order is the tracking app fee; measure WISMO tickets per 100 orders before and after, and repeat rate for the cohort.
conditions: Any DTC brand shipping parcels, especially with multi-day delivery or older or anxious buyers; tracking apps such as AfterShip, parcelLab, Malomo or Narvar.
fails_when: Same-day or next-day delivery where tracking is rarely checked; repeat-rate claims are vendor-reported and not controlled, so do not budget on them without a before-and-after test.
numbers: tracking checked about 4.6 times per order
3-step notification flow: up to 80% fewer WISMO tickets (cited claim)
branded tracking: 40 to 60% fewer WISMO contacts, 23 to 31% higher repeat rate (vendor)
Crystal Classics: WISMO calls down up to 60%; IWA: down 47%
Bokksu shipping emails: 90%+ open rate, 45.7% click-through

claim: Vendor case data: customers who took instant refunds repurchased 11x more often and 63% faster at Reebok; refunds that take 10 to 14 days lose the buyer's intent.
body: Standard refunds wait for the parcel to reach the warehouse and be inspected, often 10 to 14 days. Instant refund tools pay out (to card or store wallet) as soon as the return is booked or scanned, so the customer still has the money and the intent to rebuy while they are still shopping. Vendor-reported results compiled in the source: Reebok, using Reshop, saw 11 times higher repurchase and 63% faster repeat purchase among customers who chose instant refunds; Origin, using Loop, saw 61% fewer refund-related support tickets; Razorpay reports up to 85% retention for wallet refunds against 40 to 50% for bank refunds, and 65% faster reorders. Treat these as upper bounds: customers who choose instant refunds or store credit are already more loyal. How to apply: measure three things today: hours from return request to refund, share of refunds taken as store credit, and the share of returners who buy again within 60 days. Then pilot instant refunds or instant store credit (optionally with a small bonus) for low-risk customers, and compare 60-day repurchase against a holdout. Cost per order is the tool fee plus fraud exposure on items that never come back.
conditions: Brands with meaningful return volume (apparel, footwear, beauty) and repeat-purchase potential; Shopify-compatible returns apps.
fails_when: High return-fraud or 'wardrobing' categories, or thin-margin brands that cannot carry refunds for items not yet received; self-selection inflates the vendor numbers, so a holdout is needed before trusting the lift.

Origin via Loop: 61% fewer refund-related tickets (vendor)
Razorpay wallet refunds: up to 85% retention versus 40 to 50% for bank refunds, 65% faster reorders (vendor)

claim: At about 60% of the presenter's brands, customers acquired on deep discounts had markedly worse LTV; check cohorts by discount code and by ad angle before scaling either.
body: Discount events lower prices for people who were not buying at full price; when prices return, many do not come back. In the presenter's portfolio, roughly 60% of brands see substantially worse lifetime value from customers acquired on a high discount, though some nine-figure retailers show no difference, so check your own data. His co-host adds that $20 AOV TikTok Shop buyers and 40 to 50% off Black Friday buyers return far less than full-price customers who spent $200, and ranks retention levers in this order: product quality, product range with natural repeat or cross-sell, acquisition quality, customer experience, and only then owned media. Ad angles create the same effect: an angle that sells the product for a job it does not do well (a skin supplement advertised for energy) can show a strong ROAS on day one, then return, refund and never repurchase. How to apply: tag every first order with its discount code, offer and ad angle or persona; compare 90 and 365-day LTGP by tag; use post-purchase surveys to capture the job the buyer hired the product for; shift ad spend toward the personas, angles and offers that produce your top 20% customers, even if front-end ROAS is a little lower.
conditions: Brands with enough cohort history to compare discount and non-discount buyers; paid social accounts testing many angles.
fails_when: Brands where discount cohorts retain as well as full-price ones (some large retailers), or where the discount is the brand's permanent positioning.
numbers: about 60% of the presenter's brands see worse LTV from discount-acquired customers

claim: Do not spend delight on service failures: in Dixon's 97,000-interaction research, high-effort resolution is about 4x likelier to create disloyalty than low effort creates loyalty; remove effort first.
body: Surprise gifts and apology discounts feel like good recovery, but the research summarised in The Effortless Experience (data from over 97,000 service interactions) found that exceeding expectations during a problem adds almost no loyalty beyond simply fixing it quickly; loyalty plateaus once expectations are met. What moves loyalty is effort: a high-effort experience is roughly four times more likely to create active disloyalty than a low-effort one is to create loyalty, and perceived effort (repeating the story, being transferred, switching channels) matters as much as time taken. So split the two jobs. For broken items, late parcels, billing errors and returns, measure Customer Effort Score and first-contact resolution, let agents resolve without escalation, and anticipate the next question in the same reply. Save gifts, notes and wild bets for neutral or positive moments with high-value customers. A wild bet sent to someone who spent hours chasing a refund the week before does not repair the relationship; fix the baseline before funding delight.
conditions: Any store with a support function; most relevant when support tickets are growing or refunds and returns are slow; research base is cross-industry service data, not ecommerce-specific.
fails_when: Severe failures with real harm (allergic reaction, ruined event, lost heirloom) where a fast fix alone reads as cold and a personal gesture is expected; and luxury brands whose positioning depends on lavish recovery.
numbers: over 97,000 service interactions in the underlying study
high effort about 4x likelier to cause disloyalty than low effort to cause loyalty
asks: should we send a free gift when an order goes wrong
what actually keeps customers loyal after a complaint
our support is slow, should we add surprise and delight
what support metric matters most for retention

claim: Refund-without-return works for low-value items, usually under $20: a return can cost 20 to 65% of the item's cost to process, but about 9% of returns are fraudulent.
body: A keep-it (returnless) refund pays the customer back and lets them keep the item. The compilation cites goTRG's 2023 returns report: 59% of surveyed retailers offered keep-it refunds, up from 26% the year before, mostly for items priced up to $20. Amazon began in 2017; Chewy, Walmart, Target and Glossier use them; supplement brand O Positiv runs a 30-day money-back guarantee with no return needed. The economics: per UPS, processing a return can cost 20% to 65% of the cost of goods, sometimes up to 100%, so for cheap, perishable, damaged or hard-to-resell items, shipping it back destroys more value than it saves. The risk is abuse: NRF and Happy Returns put fraudulent returns at about 9%. How to run it: set a price threshold (refund without return under about $20), apply it case by case through support rather than advertising it as policy, and watch refund rate per customer for repeat claimers. Measure repeat-purchase rate of customers who received one against similar customers who did not. Figures are second-hand via trade press, not audited.
conditions: Low-price items (about $20 or less) where return shipping plus handling exceeds resale value; perishable, consumable or damaged goods; brands with a support team able to apply it case by case. Cost ceiling: the item's landed cost per approved claim.
fails_when: High-value or easily resold items; the policy is advertised so abuse rises beyond about 9%; no tracking of repeat claimers; marketplaces where fraud rings target keep-it policies.
numbers: 59% of surveyed retailers offered keep-it refunds in 2023, up from 26% (goTRG)
threshold usually items up to $20
return processing 20 to 65% of COGS, up to 100% (UPS)
about 9% of returns fraudulent (NRF/Happy Returns)
asks: Should I let customers keep the item instead of sending it back?

claim: Loyalty coins that expire 60 days after purchase, with expiry reminders by email and SMS, turned loss aversion into a return trigger for Indian D2C brand Haus & Kinder.
body: Most D2C loyalty schemes award points that sit untouched. Haus & Kinder, an Indian home and kids brand, awarded coins on every purchase that expired 60 days later, and sent expiry reminders by email and SMS. The reminder itself became the reason to come back: customers returned not for a new product need but to avoid losing value they felt they had earned. D2CX reports a 70x ROI on the retention tooling, and that 12.4% of all customer sign-ups came through the loyalty system, so the programme also helped acquisition. How to apply: set an expiry window that fits your natural repurchase cycle (shorter than the typical gap you want to close, but long enough to be usable), send reminders at fixed points before expiry across email and SMS, show the balance in money terms, and measure repeat rate and margin for members versus non-members. Cost per order: the value of redeemed coins plus messaging cost; set coin value so a redemption still leaves contribution margin. Treat the 70x as a newsletter-reported figure without method.
conditions: Consumables or categories with a natural repurchase within about 2 to 4 months; brands with email and SMS consent; India-reported case.
fails_when: Long repurchase cycles (furniture, electronics), where a 60-day expiry just angers customers; jurisdictions or programmes where points expiry rules are regulated or must be disclosed prominently; coin values that cut below contribution margin.
numbers: coins expire after 60 days
70x ROI on retention tooling (D2CX-reported)
12.4% of customer sign-ups via the loyalty system
asks: Should my loyalty points expire?
Our loyalty programme does not drive repeat orders, what can we change?
How long should loyalty points last before expiring?

claim: Personalised second-purchase letters to 15,000 first-time buyers doubled conversion versus a control group and returned 6x for German pet retailer Fressnapf.
body: The second purchase is the hardest one in most stores, and emails to one-time buyers compete with a crowded inbox. Fressnapf, a German pet supplies retailer, mailed personalised physical letters through optilyz to 15,000 customers who had bought once but not twice. Against a control group that did not receive the letter, the campaign doubled the conversion rate and produced an ROI of 6. Related cases in the same compilation: outdoor retailer Bergzeit's automated birthday letters, connected to its Emarsys email platform, reached a redemption rate of about 7.5%; GOLDNER's welcome letter to new club members across seven European countries converted at 3.4% to 13.6% depending on the market; thredUP raised direct-mail ROI 128% through A/B testing creative with Lob. How to apply: pick the moment a second order is most likely (the compilation suggests 30 to 60 days after the first), send a letter personalised to the first purchase with one specific offer, run it from your email or CDP triggers, track with a unique code, and always keep a holdout. Cost per order: print and postage per letter divided by incremental orders.
conditions: Retailers with postal addresses from orders and a product with natural repeat purchase (pet, food, apparel, outdoor); EU, UK and US.
fails_when: Low-margin, low-AOV single-purchase products; customers who opted out of marketing mail; figures are vendor and award-entry results without reported sample method beyond Fressnapf's control group.

Bergzeit birthday letter: about 7.5% redemption
GOLDNER welcome letter: 3.4% to 13.6% conversion across 7 countries
thredUP: +128% direct mail ROI after A/B testing (Lob)
suggested timing 30 to 60 days after first purchase
asks: How do I get first-time buyers to order again?
Should I send a letter to customers who only bought once?
What is a good win-back tactic besides email?

claim: Subscription churn spikes on day 1 (discount hunters), around day 28 (billing reminder) and days 31 to 45; Breez cut quarterly churn from 24% to 17% with giveaways and education.
body: The guest describes three churn peaks in a healthy subscription: day 1, from buyers who took the subscribe discount and cancel immediately (the largest spike); around day 28, when the billing reminder arrives; and a window from about day 31 to 45 after they have used the product. Day-1 cancellers are hard to keep, but telling them a real gift arrives in month two gives a reason to stay. The first seven days need heavy communication: what to expect, how and when to use the product, how others feel, reviews. A no-cost tactic that worked: anyone still subscribed past the 27th is entered to win five free cases. Breez reduced churn from 24% in Q4 to 17% in Q1 and aims for under 5% aggregate, which he says requires more products, flexible frequency and a lower effective price rather than tricks. Cancellation reasons cluster into four: cannot afford it, have too much, did not like the effect, found another brand. Answers include downsizing the pack or can size, showing other uses or gifting, and switching formats. Make cancelling as easy as subscribing; he notes forced minimum terms are no longer permitted, so retention has to be earned.
conditions: DTC subscription brands for consumables; churn measured monthly by cohort.
fails_when: Non-subscription products; brands that hide cancellation, which breaches consumer-protection rules in several markets and erodes trust; giveaways where prize rules or sweepstakes law are not followed.

first 7 days of heavy onboarding communication
churn 24% (Q4) to 17% (Q1)
target under 5% aggregate churn
subscribers past day 27 entered to win 5 cases

claim: True Classic set a fixed weekly 'wow budget' to win back angry customers and surprise high-LTV ones, tracking the effect through word-of-mouth share in post-purchase surveys.
body: Starting one January, True Classic gave its customer team a fixed amount of money per week to spend on two things: going overboard for customers who were upset (a gift, sometimes not even a True Classic product, chosen after learning what the person likes) and sending random surprises to top lifetime-value customers found in the CRM. The thinking, shared by the interviewer from his own brand, is that customers who receive these gestures retell the story, turning a complaint into word of mouth and making them some of the most valuable customers. Bartlett measures the payoff indirectly: the share of post-purchase survey responses naming friends or family should rise over time as these and other unscalable gestures add up. The founder also personally answers escalations that reach him. How to apply: 1) set a fixed weekly budget so spend is capped; 2) give the team simple rules on who qualifies (serious complaints, top LTV); 3) log every gesture and the customer; 4) compare repeat rate and referrals of recipients against similar customers, and watch word-of-mouth survey share. No budget size, cost per order or repeat-rate effect was given.
conditions: Brands with a CRM showing customer value and a support team able to personalise gestures.
fails_when: Without logging and comparison, the spend cannot be evaluated; gestures that customers learn to game by complaining.
asks: How do we turn angry customers into fans?
Should we have a budget for surprise gifts to customers?

claim: Under the FTC's mail order rule a US store needs a reasonable basis for any ship time it states or implies, must ship within 30 days if it states none.
body: Under the FTC's mail order rule a US store needs a reasonable basis for any ship time it states or implies, must ship within 30 days if it states none, and on a delay must notify the buyer with a free way to cancel and refund promptly. The FTC's Business Guide to the Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule says sellers must have a reasonable basis for stating or implying that they can ship within a certain time, meaning information that would satisfy a reasonable and prudent business person acting in good faith, judged on demand, supply, fulfilment capacity and records. With no shipment statement, the seller needs a reasonable basis for shipping within 30 days of a properly completed order (50 days where a credit application is involved). If a promise cannot be met, the seller must notify the buyer reasonably quickly with a revised date or an explanation, seek consent to the delay, and say the buyer may cancel instead, with a free way to do so. Required refunds must be prompt, generally within seven working days for most payment methods, and include shipping charges; store credit does not count. How to apply: every cutoff date, 'ships in 24 hours' line or gift-delivery promise must come from the store's real dispatch records, and a delay message template with a cancel option must exist before a peak.
conditions: US orders taken online, by phone or by mail.
fails_when: Non-US orders follow local consumer law; the rule governs shipment, not carrier transit, so delivery-date promises also need carrier performance data.
numbers: 30 days default when no ship time is stated
Refunds generally within 7 working days
asks: Can I promise delivery before Christmas on my site?
What do I have to do if orders ship late in the US?
Is it legal to say ships in 24 hours if we sometimes miss it?

evidence.where: Sections on shipment statements, delay notices and refunds

claim: In Baymard's 2022 benchmark, 83% of desktop and 87% of mobile apparel sites gave insufficient sizing information; uncertainty about size was a common reason test users abandoned a product.
body: Baymard's large-scale usability testing of apparel sites found nearly all sites offer some sizing information but only 17% of desktop and 13% of mobile sites offer enough. In testing, users hesitated to buy when unsure of their size, and an item that does not fit has to be returned, which costs the buyer effort and loads support. Baymard's ten sizing practices: show conventional sizes (S, M, L) or a conversion to them; numeric sizes where the product type uses them; measurements in both inches and centimetres; international size conversions; instructions for taking body measurements; sizing tailored to the product type (ideally by brand); a prominent size guide link next to the size selector; the browser Back button closing the guide and returning to the product; a link to support or chat inside the guide; and model measurements plus the size the model wears next to on-model images. How to apply: build the guide per product type from real garment measurements and the store's return reasons, and place it beside the size picker.
conditions: Apparel, footwear and accessories sold online, desktop and mobile.
fails_when: The benchmark is from 2022, so shares may have moved; products without sizing (one-size goods) need a use or fit guide instead.
numbers: 83% of desktop and 87% of mobile apparel sites gave insufficient sizing information
Ten sizing practices

claim: Shopify return rules set a window (none, 14, 30, 90 days, unlimited or custom) from delivery, per-product overrides where the shortest wins, return shipping and restocking fees, and final sale items.
body: Shopify return rules let a store choose no returns, 14, 30 or 90 days, unlimited or a custom number of days, counted from each item's delivery or from delivery of the last item in the order, with an option to extend to the next business day. Collections, products or variants can have their own window; if an item sits in several overrides the shortest window applies. Return shipping can be free, a flat fee charged once per return, or a label the buyer buys. A restocking fee is a percentage shown when the buyer asks for a return, but fees are not deducted from refunds automatically, so staff must deduct them when refunding. Products or collections can be marked final sale; bundles cannot. Self-serve returns, where buyers request returns from their account, is a separate setting, and return rules still apply to returns made by staff. Cancellation windows are set separately: none, until fulfilled, 15 minutes, 1 hour or 24 hours.
conditions: Shopify stores as described in the help article on the date fetched.
fails_when: The store runs returns through a third-party returns app with its own rules, or local law sets a minimum right that overrides the store's window.

shortest override window applies
cancellation window options: none, until fulfilled, 15 minutes, 1 hour, 24 hours

claim: Google's review policy bars merchants from offering any incentive for reviews, asking only happy customers, discouraging negative reviews, or setting staff quotas for reviews.
body: Google's Maps user generated content policy lists, under fake engagement, that merchants may not offer incentives such as payment, discounts, free goods or services for reviews (or for removing a negative one), may not discourage or prohibit negative reviews or selectively solicit positive reviews, and may not ask staff to collect a set number of reviews. Content based on a conflict of interest, including current or former employment, is not allowed. For a store, this means a Google review ask must go to every eligible buyer with the same wording and no reward, and no survey may sit in front of it to filter out unhappy buyers.
conditions: Reviews on Google (Business Profile and Maps). Applies to any store that asks buyers to review it on Google.
fails_when: Reviews on the store's own site or other platforms follow their own rules; an incentive allowed by the FTC for an on-site review is still banned for a Google review.

claim: The FTC says review incentives are allowed only with no stated or implied sentiment required; asking only happy buyers may break the FTC Act; intimidation to remove reviews is banned; site moderation must treat good and bad reviews equally.
body: The FTC's November 2024 questions and answers on its consumer reviews rule say: the rule has no specific ban on asking only satisfied customers for reviews, but the practice could violate the FTC Act under the Endorsement Guides. Incentives for reviews are allowed as long as there is no express or implied requirement for a particular sentiment; 'tell us how much you loved it and get a coupon' implies one. A business must not use threats or intimidation, which includes abusive messages and character attacks, to get a review removed or changed. A store may keep some reviews off its own site (for example ones about other products, or only about customer service) only if the rule is applied equally to positive and negative reviews. Courts can impose civil penalties for knowing violations.
conditions: US buyers and US-facing stores; reviews on the store's own site, emails and ads.
fails_when: Other platforms (Google, Amazon) can be stricter than the FTC, for example banning incentives outright.

claim: WhatsApp allows automated replies but requires prompt, clear and direct escalation paths to a person, such as in-chat human transfer, phone, email, web support or a form.
body: The WhatsApp Business Messaging Policy (page updated 23 September 2026) says a business may use automation when responding during the 24-hour window, but must also have prompt, clear and direct escalation paths available. It lists in-chat human agent transfer, phone number, email, web support, in-store visits and a support form. It also says a business may contact people only if they gave their number and opted in to receive messages, and recommends separate opt-in by message category. For a store chatbot on WhatsApp this makes a working human handoff a policy requirement, not a nice-to-have.

fails_when: Other chat channels (site chat, Instagram) have their own rules; the handoff is still good practice there.

claim: Under the FTC's Endorsement Guides, a reward that could change how much weight people give a recommendation must be disclosed, and the advertiser must train and monitor the people it rewards.
body: The FTC's 'What people are asking' guidance says that if a reward could affect the weight or credibility readers give an endorsement, it should be disclosed, and that even an incentive with no money value may need disclosure. For network programs it advises telling members to disclose free products and checking periodically that they do; advertisers need reasonable programs to train and monitor the people they pay or reward. For a referral program, a customer who posts a referral link publicly for a reward should say they get something, and the store should tell them so and check.
conditions: US-facing referral, affiliate and ambassador programs where customers post or share for a reward.
fails_when: A private one-to-one share between friends who know about the reward carries less risk; the guidance does not name refer-a-friend programs directly.

claim: Net Promoter Score asks how likely someone is to recommend the brand on a 0 to 10 scale; 9 to 10 are promoters, 7 to 8 passives, 0 to 6 detractors, and NPS is percent promoters minus percent detractors.
body: Bain's 2011 introduction of the Net Promoter System defines the question as how likely it is that you would recommend the product, service or company to a friend or colleague, scored 0 to 10. Promoters score 9 or 10, passives 7 or 8 and detractors 0 to 6. The score is the percentage of promoters minus the percentage of detractors; passives count in the base but not in the score, so NPS runs from minus 100 to plus 100. Because 0 to 6 are all detractors, a 6 and a 0 move the score the same way, which is why the follow-up comment and a fast reply to low scorers matter more than the number.
conditions: Any store running a recommend-likelihood survey and comparing scores over time.
fails_when: Small samples swing the score; comparisons across brands or survey timings are unreliable.

detractors 0 to 6

claim: India's dark pattern guidelines treat hard or hidden cancellation, requiring payment details for auto-debit during a free subscription, and charging recurring payments without the user's knowledge, such as an unannounced trial-to-paid switch or auto-renewal, as dark patterns.
body: Khaitan & Co. summarise two subscription patterns from the CCPA's 2023 guidelines. A subscription trap is requiring payment details for auto-debits during a free subscription, or making cancellation hard through complicated steps or a hidden cancel button. SaaS billing is collecting recurring payments in a software-as-a-service model without the user's consent or knowledge, for example not telling users when a free trial becomes paid, or auto-renewing without notice. Nagging, a separate pattern, covers repeated prompts the user has not agreed to. For a store with subscribe and save, refills or memberships, the subscription trap pattern is the one that clearly applies. How to apply: put a cancel button in the customer account that works in as few steps as it took to subscribe; do not hide it behind chat or phone calls; if a free trial needs a card, state the charge date and amount before sign-up; send a reminder before each renewal or trial conversion; and keep records of consent to recurring charges.
conditions: Subscriptions, memberships and free trials offered to consumers in India.
fails_when: SaaS billing is written for software services; physical product subscriptions may be judged under the subscription trap pattern instead. RBI rules on recurring card mandates also apply. This is a law-firm summary.
asks: How easy must subscription cancellation be in India?
Can I ask for card details for a free trial in India?
Do I need to remind customers before a subscription renews in India?

claim: In India, an online seller cannot refuse to take back goods or refund if they are defective, deficient, spurious, not as advertised, or delivered later than the stated schedule (unless force majeure).
body: Rule 7(4) of the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 says no inventory e-commerce entity may refuse to take back goods, or refuse to refund what was paid, where the goods are defective, deficient or spurious, do not have the characteristics or features advertised or agreed, or arrive late against the stated delivery schedule. Late delivery caused by force majeure is excused. Rule 6(3) puts the same duty on sellers on a marketplace. Rule 4(10) requires refunds on accepted requests to be paid within a reasonable time or as the Reserve Bank of India or other law prescribes. So a 'no returns' policy is fine for change-of-mind returns, but it cannot block returns or refunds in these cases. How to apply: write the returns policy in two parts, a statutory part (faulty, wrong, not as described or late: always accepted) and a goodwill part (change of mind, with any window and conditions you choose), and state realistic delivery dates, because a promised date you miss becomes a refund right.
conditions: Online sales to consumers in India, own site or marketplace.
fails_when: Change-of-mind returns, which the rules leave to the seller's policy; delays caused by force majeure.
asks: Can I have a no returns policy in India?
Does a late delivery mean I have to refund in India?
Do I have to refund a customer if the product doesn't match the photos?
How fast must I refund customers in India?
